summary.text: Cholesterol is the principal sterol of all animals and an essential structural and signaling component of animal cell membranes.
All animal cells make it, and in vertebrates hepatic cells typically produce the greatest amounts, while it is absent among prokaryotes with a few exceptions.
It is also a precursor for steroid hormones, bile acid and vitamin D, and high blood levels bound to LDL may increase cardiovascular disease risk.

facts.label: First found
facts.value: In gallstones, in solid form, in 1769

facts.label: Name origin
facts.value: Greek words for bile and solid, plus the suffix -ol

facts.label: Daily synthesis
facts.value: About 1 gram a day in a 68 kg man

facts.label: Body total
facts.value: About 35 g, mostly within cell membranes

items.prompt: A man eats a cholesterol-rich meal. Why does it have little effect on his blood cholesterol hours later?

options.label: Stomach acid destroys nearly all of it first
The gallbladder stores all of it permanently
It is converted into phytosterols in the gut
Most is poorly absorbed, and the body cuts its own synthesis

items.explain: Most ingested cholesterol is esterified and poorly absorbed, and the body compensates by reducing its own synthesis.

items.prompt: A man eats a lot of cholesterol-rich food. Where does his brain get the cholesterol it uses?

options.label: Hepatic cells send it straight to the neurons through the blood
Astrocytes make it there, since dietary cholesterol cannot cross in
Neurons absorb it directly from the gut
Blood carries it across the barrier after absorption

items.explain: Under normal conditions brain cholesterol is separate from peripheral cholesterol; astrocytes produce and distribute it in the brain.

items.prompt: Plants and most bacteria build cell walls. What lets animal cells hold together without one?

options.label: A hardened membrane that never changes shape
Plant sterols that stand in for a wall
Cholesterol packs the membrane, keeping it intact but not rigid
A coat of extra fatty acids on the outside

items.explain: Cholesterol increases membrane packing, maintaining integrity so animal cells do not need walls, while the membrane stays stable without being rigid.

items.prompt: A statin drug slows the body's own cholesterol production. Which part of making it does the drug target?

options.label: The first 18 steps, the mevalonate (HMG-CoA reductase) pathway
The last 19 steps that convert lanosterol
Absorption of ingested cholesterol in the gut
Transport of cholesterol in the blood by LDL

items.explain: De novo synthesis begins with the mevalonate or HMG-CoA reductase pathway, the target of statin drugs, which covers the first 18 steps.

items.prompt: Plants make large amounts of chemicals similar to cholesterol. What might these do in a person's intestines?

options.label: Turn into cholesterol before it can be absorbed
Block astrocytes from making brain cholesterol
Raise reabsorption of cholesterol from the gut
Compete with cholesterol for reabsorption, possibly lowering it

items.explain: Phytosterols are chemically similar to cholesterol and compete with it for reabsorption in the intestinal tract, potentially reducing cholesterol reabsorption.

items.prompt: Cholesterol is implicated in cell signaling. What does it help form in the plasma membrane to do this?

options.label: Cell walls that anchor the receptors in place
Lipid rafts that bring receptor proteins near second messengers
Ion pumps that carry second messengers across
Extra mitochondria that power the receptors

items.explain: Cholesterol assists in forming lipid rafts, which bring receptor proteins in close proximity with high concentrations of second messenger molecules.
